name: Protection Detail Log: 72 Hours
author: Redacted per subject's request
description: Personal operational log kept by a B-tier freelancer during a 72-hour close protection detail in the Gray Zone district 14, GLMZ North Corridor. Client was a community organizer named Petra Solís, involved in blocking a Harken-Yusef Holdings rezoning proposal that would have displaced approximately 4,200 residents. The freelancer retained this log and submitted a redacted copy to their broker as a professional record. Document circulates occasionally in freelancer forums as an example of non-standard threat assessment on low-budget residential contracts.
body:
PROTECTION DETAIL — PERSONAL LOG Client: [REDACTED] Location: the Gray Zone-14, North Corridor, GLMZ Duration: 72 hours contracted Rate: Φ340 flat, Φ80 hazard trigger (never paid out, see notes) Broker: Osei

---

HOUR 00:00

Client's name is Petra. She told me that herself, first thing, which already made her different from most people who hire protection they can barely afford. Usually there's a performance of distance. She didn't do that. She's maybe fifty, maybe older — hard to tell in the Gray Zone, the air takes years off people fast and puts different ones back on. Her apartment is three rooms on the 34th stack, the Gray Zone-14. The kind of place where the ventilation hums constantly and you stop hearing it after six minutes.

I walked the space. One entrance, window egress to a maintenance ledge, neighbor on the left is a woman named Hana who Petra vouches for, neighbor on the right is a unit that's been empty for three weeks. I noted the empty unit. Asked Petra if she knew why. She said the family left after someone left a melted plastic token on their welcome mat. Harken-Yusef Holdings uses subcontractors for that kind of message work. Low-cost intimidation. Efficient.

We established protocols. She does not leave without me or without telling me exactly where and for how long. I sleep in four-hour rotations on her couch. She does not answer her door. She does not take food deliveries from anyone she didn't personally order from. She seemed frustrated by the last one — apparently she'd been coordinating meals for the block committee. I told her we could build in a verification step. She agreed. She's practical. I appreciated that.

Before I let her go to bed, I asked who knew I'd been hired. She said her daughter, two members of the block committee, and her broker contact who arranged the job. I wrote all four names down.

---

HOUR 06:15

First incident. Not what I expected.

Knock at the door, 0615. Not aggressive. Petra is asleep. I check the hall cam on my overlay — a man, 30s, holding a data chip and looking nervous. I don't open the door. I ask through the panel who he is.

He says he's from the block committee. He says he has survey data Petra needs before her 0900 call with the rezoning mediator. He says it's important.

I ask his name. He gives it. I ping Petra's comm — she picks up fast, she wasn't really sleeping. She confirms the name but she sounds uncertain. I ask her: did you arrange for him to come at 0615? She pauses. No.

I tell him through the panel that she'll connect with him after 0900. He argues for three minutes. Then he leaves.

I note: the survey data could be real. The timing is either careless or it's a probe to see how we respond to unexpected contact. I don't know which. I tell Petra that I don't know which and that we're going to treat it as a probe until we have reason not to.

She says: "You're not going to tell me it was probably fine?"

I say: "No."

She seems to find this more reassuring than the alternative would have been.

---

HOUR 14:00 — HOUR 26:00

Nothing.

This is where it gets hard. Not dangerous-hard. Boring-hard. The kind of tired that isn't about sleep, it's about the specific weight of watching a door that doesn't open and listening to a ventilation hum that never changes pitch and eating a nutrition brick that tastes like compressed apology.

Petra works through the day. She's on her comm constantly — the 0900 call goes two hours, she's got mediator prep, she's coordinating with two other block committees in the Gray Zone-11 and the Gray Zone-17 who are facing the same rezoning wave. She moves between her kitchen table and a chair by the window and she talks with her hands and occasionally she gets very quiet for about sixty seconds and then she starts again.

I watch the door. I watch the hall cam. I watch the empty unit across on the cam feed I pulled from maintenance access.

At hour 19 I let myself think about whether this job matters. I try not to do that, usually. It's not useful and it costs something I don't always have budget for. But it was a long stretch and I did it anyway.

Here's what I came up with: 4,200 people live in the Gray Zone-14. Harken-Yusef wants to rezone two of the lower stacks for vertical logistics infrastructure — automated warehousing, drone corridors. They've done it in the Gray Zone-6 and the Gray Zone-9. The displaced residents in the Gray Zone-6 are in temporary overflow stacking in the Gray Zone-3, which is worse. Some of them are still there, two years later. Petra knows all of this. She's been working this block for eleven years.

I'm being paid Φ340 to keep her alive for 72 hours. Harken-Yusef's legal team probably costs Φ340 every six minutes. I note this and then I stop noting things like this because it isn't useful.

---

HOUR 51:00

This is the one.

Three men in the hallway at 0330. My hall cam caught them coming up from the maintenance level — not the resident elevators. They're not uniformed. No Arcturus insignia. Subcontractors, which meant they had deniability and loose instructions, which is actually more dangerous than a formal enforcement action in some ways.

I woke Petra. Told her to go to her bathroom, lock it, and stay there until I said otherwise. She went.

I positioned at the door. Not behind it — off to the side, with a line to the window egress if I needed it.

They knocked. When I didn't answer they used a bypass tool on the panel, which told me they had at least mid-grade corporate subcontract gear. The door unsealed.

Here is what I did not do: I did not shoot anyone.

Here is what I did do: I turned the lights on and I was standing there with a sidearm visible and my overlay running active ID-capture on all three of their faces, and I said, clearly, that I had already transmitted their biometric profiles to three separate dead-drop addresses, and that if this escalated to a use-of-force incident, those profiles would be routed to every broker in the North Corridor by morning.

The man in front — older, the kind of tired that's different from my tired — he looked at me for a long time.

I said: "She's not here tonight. Come back with paperwork."

I did not say whether that was true.

He said: "We're not here to hurt her."

I said: "I know. You're here to scare her. It's not going to work. But someone's going to make a mistake in the next thirty seconds if we keep standing here, and then we're all going to have a worse week than we planned."

Another long pause.

They left. The door was left open. I sealed it manually and held position until 0600.

---

HOUR 72:00

Contract end.

Petra made coffee and offered me a chair and asked me what I thought would happen next. I told her honestly that I didn't know. The subcontractors would report back. Harken-Yusef's people would have to decide if another approach was worth the exposure. The mediator call was still scheduled. None of that was guaranteed to go any particular way.

She asked if I'd take another contract if she could afford one.

I told her I was already booked but to go through Osei and ask about availability in two weeks.

I meant it. Which surprised me a little.

I walked out at 0847. Took the stairs. Thought about the man at the door, how tired he looked, how he said they weren't there to hurt her like he needed me to believe it. Maybe he did. Doesn't change what he was there to do.

Φ340 in account by 0900. Osei takes his cut. I get Φ298.

I bought a meal that didn't taste like compressed apology. That's something.

---

Notes for broker record: Client conducted herself professionally throughout. Threat profile was subcontract intimidation, mid-grade, no indication of authorization for physical harm at this stage. Recommend continued monitoring. Would work with client again.

Personal notes, not for broker: I keep thinking about the empty apartment next door. The family that got the melted token and left. Nobody hired protection for them. Probably couldn't afford it. Probably never occurred to anyone to offer.

I don't have a conclusion for that. I'm just writing it down.
